title: Collaborative documents
brief: Many people edit the same document at the same moment and everyone must see a consistent result in a fraction of a second. Edits must never be lost, even if a server crashes in the middle of typing or two people type in the same place.

clarify.q: What if two people edit the same sentence together?
clarify.a: Both edits survive and everyone ends up with the same text. The order of edits is decided in one place per document.

clarify.q: How fast must an edit reach others?
clarify.a: Under about 250 ms, counting the trip across an ocean. More than that and cursors feel jumpy.

clarify.q: What if someone loses their connection?
clarify.a: They keep typing offline and their edits merge when they return.
Never. Typed text is saved before it is confirmed.

notes: 250,000 people editing at once, about a tenth typing in any one second (approx.).
One gateway node holds about 100,000 open connections (approx.).

text.name: Synchronized rush
text.description: Many callers send requests together instead of spreading them over time.

debrief.headline: A synchronized rush hit {node}.
debrief.fix: Spread scheduled work over time and keep spare capacity on the affected path. A rate limiter protects downstream work by rejecting excess calls, so it cannot by itself meet every availability target.

numbers.label: Socket gateway nodes needed
numbers.how: 250,000 open connections ÷ 100,000 each ≈ 3; use 4 for spare room (approx.)

hints: Two people editing the same document must agree on the order. Where does that order get decided?
Send every edit to one server per document over a socket, write it to a log first, then fan it out. Save snapshots from time to time.
Compaction must preserve convergence and the supported offline boundary. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Each open document has one owner server that orders all the edits. Edits are written to a durable log in several zones before they are confirmed, then sent out to everyone. Snapshots saved now and then keep opening a document quick.

designs.name: Owner per document with a durable log
designs.why: The coordination service decides which server owns each document. Edits go into a log replicated over three zones, so nothing is lost if a zone falls over. A background pipeline writes snapshots so opening a document never replays millions of edits.

tradeoffs: One owner per document gives a clear order but is a single point to recover. The coordination service picks a new owner within seconds.
Writing to the log before confirming adds a few milliseconds but means no typed text is ever lost.
Snapshots speed up opening a document at the cost of storage and a background job.
Offline edits are merged by a rule that keeps both sides' work. It is clever, and hard to explain to users.
editorial.realWorld: Editors in the real world serve millions of simultaneous documents. Each document is small, and the per-document activity is modest; the difficulty is the sheer number of sockets and the ordering (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Collaborative documents: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Converge concurrent edits and recover durable operations across reconnects. Convergence requires a shared conflict rule, not just fast sockets. Deduplication belongs with durable operation persistence. Compaction must preserve convergence and the supported offline boundary.

fields.label: Step 1. Two users insert at the same position on version 12. What resolves it?
options: Apply each client’s local arrival order
A defined transform or CRDT ordering with stable operation ids
fields.explanation: Convergence requires a shared conflict rule, not just fast sockets.

fields.label: Step 2. The edit commits but acknowledgement is lost. Retry how?
options: Resend its operation id and receive the committed result
fields.explanation: Deduplication belongs with durable operation persistence.

fields.label: Step 3. A client reconnects after a snapshot was compacted. What recovers its edits?
options: Discard unsent edits because the old log is gone
A compatible snapshot and operation frontier, with a defined rebase or merge
fields.explanation: Compaction must preserve convergence and the supported offline boundary.

correctness.responsibility: Converge concurrent edits and recover durable operations across reconnects.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.
